title: San Jose Woman Arrested on Hate Crime Charges After Accusing Dad of Trafficking Daughter
excerpt: The 47-year-old was booked into Santa Clara County jail on suspicion of stalking and hate crimes after a viral video showed her confronting a father in San Jose's Almaden neighborhood over his 6-year-old daughter.
body:
• San Jose police arrested a 47-year-old woman on Thursday and booked her into the Santa Clara County Main Jail on suspicion of stalking, hate crimes and other offenses.
  • The arrest followed a September 6 confrontation in the city's Almaden neighborhood, captured on video by the father and posted to TikTok, in which the woman accused him of trafficking his 6-year-old daughter because the girl appeared white and he is a man of color.
  • Investigators used automated license-plate-reader cameras to identify her vehicle and linked her to other incidents, including a confrontation at a South San Jose high school three days later.
  • The woman was reported missing by her family in 2022, and a relative cited significant mental-health issues — background police noted while the criminal investigation continues.

The viral confrontation

A 47-year-old San Jose woman was arrested Thursday and booked into the Santa Clara County Main Jail on suspicion of stalking, hate crimes and other offenses, after a video of her confronting a father and his young daughter went viral on TikTok. The encounter took place on September 6 in the city's Almaden neighborhood. The father, who had never seen the woman before, filmed the exchange and posted it online.

In the footage, the woman repeatedly approaches the father from her car and accuses him of sex trafficking his 6-year-old daughter — because, she says, the girl appears white while he is a man of color. "I believe you're either buying or selling or trafficking this child," she tells him. The father tries to walk away; she circles back and confronts him again, at one point questioning his legal status in the country. He described feeling unsettled by the encounter and has requested anonymity for his family, sharing his account publicly to raise awareness about the impact of such confrontations.

"I believe you're either buying or selling or trafficking this child."

— the woman, in the viral video, as reported by the Times of India

A pattern, not an isolated incident

San Jose police say the September 6 incident was part of a broader pattern. Their investigation linked the woman to other episodes in the area, including a confrontation at a South San Jose high school three days later that prompted a district safety alert. Using automated license-plate-reader technology, officers identified her vehicle and connected it to multiple reports of similar behavior before the department's assaults unit took her into custody.

Authorities have disclosed no evidence supporting the trafficking allegation, and police continue to treat the episode as a suspicious circumstance and a hate incident. Reporting has also surfaced background on the suspect: her family reported her missing in 2022, and a relative cited significant mental-health issues — details police have noted as context while the criminal investigation proceeds.

Why it matters

The case has drawn sharp scrutiny precisely because the accusation was built on appearance alone. Civil-rights advocates say it illustrates how racial profiling can turn an ordinary family outing into a confrontation with lasting trauma for the child involved — and how social media can amplify an unverified accusation before any facts are established. The San Jose Police Department has urged the public to report suspicious activity responsibly and avoid making assumptions based on race or appearance.

Diaspora angle

For Bay Area immigrant families — including the region's large South Asian community — the episode hits close to home. Mixed-race families, adoptive parents and fathers out alone with their children describe exactly this fear: that a stranger's snap judgment about who "belongs" together can escalate into a police matter. The father's decision to share his story, despite seeking anonymity, was aimed at those families.

What to watch

The assaults unit's investigation remains active, and police are seeking more information from the public — additional incidents could bring additional charges. Prosecutors will now decide how the stalking and hate-crime allegations proceed through Santa Clara County courts.
